questions.prompt: The covariance of a random vector \(x\) with mean \(\mu\) is
options: \(\mathbb{E}[(x-\mu)(x-\mu)^T]\), which is symmetric
\(\mathbb{E}[x]\), the mean itself
\(\mathbb{E}[x]\,\mathbb{E}[x]^T\), the outer product of the mean
the matrix \(A\) in a later linear map, before any data
questions.explanation: Covariance is the expected outer product of the centered vector, so it is symmetric and its diagonal entries are variances. The mean is a different summary. The outer product of the mean is not centered, and a matrix that will later multiply \(x\) is not the covariance of \(x\).

questions.prompt: A scalar Gaussian has variance 4. An instrument reports \(3\) times that variable. The variance of the report is
questions.explanation: A scale factor \(c\) multiplies the variance by \(c^2\). Here \(3^2 \times 4 = 36\). Multiplying the variance by \(3\) instead of \(9\) leaves the square off. Adding \(3\) to the variance treats the scale as a shift. Reporting \(4\) ignores the instrument.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded elliptical cloud of a random vector</title><line x1="28" y1="108" x2="256" y2="108"/><polygon points="256,108 249.6,110.7 249.6,105.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="124" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="28" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="108" rx="88" ry="48" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.12"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A shaded ellipse centered at the origin of two axes.

questions.prompt: Two components are independent, with variances \(2\) and \(5\). The variance of \(x_1 + 2 x_2\) is
questions.explanation: Independence kills the cross term, so the variance is \(1^2 \times 2 + 2^2 \times 5 = 22\). Using the coefficients without squares gives \(2 + 2 \times 5 = 12\). Adding the variances with no coefficients gives \(7\). The product \(2 \times 5 = 10\) is neither term.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two independent component variances</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">2   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   5</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with 2 and 5 on the diagonal and zeros off it.

questions.prompt: A scalar Gaussian \(z\) has variance \(v\). Write the variance of \(c z\) in the names \(c\) and \(v\).
questions.explanation: The scale comes out twice because covariance is an outer product: \(\mathrm{Var}(c z) = c^2 v\). The form \(c v\) forgets one factor. The form \(c + v\) treats the scale as a shift, and a shift does not change a variance.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a level curve of a covariance, longer on the first axis</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: An ellipse centered on the axes, stretched farther along the first coordinate.

questions.prompt: Let \(P = \mathrm{diag}(3, 5)\) and \(A = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\). The top-left entry of \(A P A^T\) is
questions.explanation: \(A P = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 10 \\ 3 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(A^T = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ 2 & 0 \end{bmatrix}\), so the top-left entry is \(10 \times 2 = 20\). Stopping at \(A P\) and reading its corner gives \(0\). Using \(A P\) without the transpose and taking the other diagonal entry of \(A P A^T\) gives \(3\), which is the image of the first variance, not this corner.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>two axis directions before a linear map</title><line x1="46" y1="161.7" x2="250" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="250,161.7 243.6,164.4 243.6,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="60.1" y1="176" x2="60.1" y2="28"/><polygon points="60.1,28 62.8,34.4 57.3,34.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="248" y="175.7" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="66.1" y="30" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="235.9" y2="161.7"/><polygon points="235.9,161.7 229.5,164.4 229.5,159" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="243.9" y="153.7" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">e1</text><line x1="60.1" y1="161.7" x2="60.1" y2="42.3"/><polygon points="60.1,42.3 62.8,48.8 57.3,48.8" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="68.1" y="34.3" text-anchor="middle" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">e2</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: Two arrows from the origin, one along each axis.

questions.prompt: Put these steps in the order you would use them to get the covariance of \(A x + d\) for a fixed matrix \(A\) and a fixed vector \(d\).
questions.explanation: A shift changes the mean and not \(P\), so it leaves first. \(P\) is the object the linear map acts on. The image covariance is \(A P A^T\), and only then do the diagonal entries become the new variances. Multiplying by \(A\) before you have \(P\) has nothing to transform.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a diagonal covariance</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">3   0</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">0   5</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 matrix with 3 and 5 on the diagonal and zeros off it.
steps: Drop the added vector d. A constant shift does not change the covariance.
Center x by its mean and form the covariance P.
Multiply on the left by A and on the right by A transpose.
Read the diagonal of that product as the variances of the components.

questions.prompt: \(x\) is a random vector with covariance \(P\), and \(A\) is a fixed square matrix. One step is wrong.
questions.explanation: Square or not, the covariance of \(A x\) is \(A P A^T\). The first two steps are the definition, and a constant shift really does drop out. The third step drops the transpose, which is exactly the factor that puts the second \(A\) on the other side of the outer product.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 200 130" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a covariance with a nonzero cross term</title><text x="28" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">[</text><text x="168" y="78" text-anchor="middle" font-size="28" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">]</text><text x="98" y="58" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">4   1</text><text x="98" y="86" text-anchor="middle" font-size="16" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">1   9</text></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A 2 by 2 symmetric matrix with 4 and 9 on the diagonal.
steps: \(P\) is symmetric, because it is an expected outer product of a centered vector.
Each diagonal entry of \(P\) is the variance of one component.
The covariance of \(A x\) is \(A P\). The transpose factor cancels because \(A\) is square.
Adding a constant vector to \(x\) leaves \(P\) unchanged.
reasons: The image covariance is A P A transpose, and a square A does not remove the transpose.
A square matrix always satisfies A P = P.
A constant shift replaces P by the outer product of the shift.

questions.prompt: For a Gaussian vector, a zero cross-covariance between two components means
options: the components have equal variance
the components are independent
the mean of each component is zero
every linear image of the vector is constant
questions.explanation: Jointly Gaussian and uncorrelated implies independent. Equal variance is a statement about the diagonal. The mean is a separate parameter. A nondegenerate Gaussian still has a spread after a linear map that keeps both directions.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a shaded elliptical cloud of a random vector</title><line x1="28" y1="108" x2="256" y2="108"/><polygon points="256,108 249.6,110.7 249.6,105.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="124" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="28" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="108" rx="88" ry="48" fill="currentColor" fill-opacity="0.12"/></svg>
questions.figure_alt: A shaded ellipse centered at the origin of two axes.

questions.prompt: Which statements hold for a covariance \(P\) and a fixed matrix \(A\)?
options: The covariance of \(A x\) is \(A P A^T\).
Adding a constant vector to \(x\) changes \(P\).
If the vector is Gaussian, uncorrelated components are independent.
A diagonal entry of \(P\) may be negative and still be a variance.
questions.explanation: The linear image sends \(P\) to \(A P A^T\). A constant changes the mean only. For a Gaussian, a zero cross term is independence, not merely a lack of linear correlation. A variance is an expected square, so a diagonal entry cannot be negative.
questions.figure: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 280 210" role="img" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.6" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round" font-family="sans-serif" font-size="12"><title>a level curve of a covariance, longer on the first axis</title><line x1="28" y1="104" x2="256" y2="104"/><polygon points="256,104 249.6,106.7 249.6,101.3" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><line x1="140" y1="186" x2="140" y2="24"/><polygon points="140,24 142.7,30.4 137.3,30.4" fill="currentColor" stroke="none"/><text x="250" y="120" text-anchor="end" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x1</text><text x="148" y="20" text-anchor="start" font-size="11" fill="currentColor" stroke="none">x2</text><ellipse cx="140" cy="104" rx="86" ry="46"/><line x1="54" y1="104" x2="226" y2="104" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/><line x1="140" y1="58" x2="140" y2="150" stroke-dasharray="4 3"/></svg>

questions.prompt: A predicted covariance is about to be formed as \(A P A^T + Q\) with \(A = 0.5\), \(P = 1\), and \(Q = 0.1\), all scalars. The predicted variance is
questions.explanation: \(0.5^2 \times 1 + 0.1 = 0.35\). Dropping the square on \(0.5\) gives \(0.6\). Forgetting \(Q\) leaves \(0.25\). Adding \(A\) itself to \(P\) gives \(1.5\), which is not a covariance update.

questions.prompt: A later recursion predicts a state by multiplying the estimate by \(A\) and the covariance by the same pattern. The covariance piece uses \(A P A^T\) because
options: \(A\) is always symmetric, so \(A P\) is enough
the mean and the covariance are the same matrix
the covariance of a linear image is the congruence \(A P A^T\)
adding process noise replaces \(P\) by \(A\)
questions.explanation: That identity is the whole content of the linear-image rule, and the predict step is where a filter spends it. Symmetry of \(A\) is not assumed. The mean is a vector. Process noise is added after the congruence, and it does not replace the map.

questions.prompt: An affine map \(x \mapsto A x + d\) of a Gaussian vector is
options: no longer Gaussian, because a shift breaks the bell shape
Gaussian only when \(A\) is diagonal
Gaussian in the mean and uniform in the covariance
still Gaussian, with mean \(A\mu + d\) and covariance \(A P A^T\)
questions.explanation: Affine images preserve the Gaussian family. The shift lands in the mean. The matrix lands in the covariance as \(A P A^T\). Diagonal \(A\) is a special case, not the condition, and the covariance is not replaced by a uniform spread.
